narration:
Imagine throwing a stone into a dark cave in the desert, and hearing something shatter inside. According to the most common account, that is how it began, in the winter of 1946 to 1947. A young shepherd was searching for a lost goat in the cliffs above the Dead Sea. He threw a stone into a small opening in the rock, heard clay break, and later climbed in with his cousins. Inside stood tall clay jars with lids. And inside some of those jars were old leather scrolls, wrapped in linen. They did not know it yet, but they had found some of the oldest surviving copies of the Bible ever discovered.

Mystery number one: how old were they? At first, almost nobody believed the scrolls could be ancient. The shepherds sold them to an antiquities dealer in Bethlehem for very little money, and from there they passed from hand to hand. Four of the first scrolls were bought by the head of a monastery in Jerusalem. Three others were bought by a professor in Jerusalem, who was one of the first to suspect how old they really were. Remember those four scrolls, because they will come back later in this story. When scholars finally saw them, they compared the shape of the letters with other ancient writing, and the style looked far older than anyone expected. Later, scientists tested the material with radiocarbon dating. Most scholars now date the scrolls from about three centuries before the time of Jesus to the decades after it. That means some of them were copied more than two thousand years ago. Over the next ten years, searchers found more caves, eleven in total. A few held complete scrolls. Most held fragments, tens of thousands of pieces, some smaller than a fingernail. Putting them back together took decades, like a jigsaw puzzle with most of the pieces missing.

Mystery number two: how did they survive? Leather and parchment usually rot away. These scrolls were made from animal skins, written with ink made from soot, in neat columns, with reed pens. Then they spent two thousand years in some of the driest air on Earth. The desert around the Dead Sea gets very little rain, and the caves stayed dark and still. Some scrolls were sealed in jars, which protected them even more. Others simply lay on the cave floor, where insects, rodents and time slowly ate them away. That is why one cave can hold a nearly perfect scroll, while another holds only crumbs of writing.

Mystery number three: what did they say? Scholars have identified close to a thousand different manuscripts. Most are written in Hebrew, with some in Aramaic and a few in Greek. Many of them are copies of books from the Hebrew Bible, and fragments of almost every book have been found. Others are prayers, hymns, commentaries, calendars and rules for a religious community. The most famous is the Great Isaiah Scroll. It is more than seven meters long, and it contains the whole book of Isaiah. Before these discoveries, the oldest known Hebrew copies of Isaiah were about a thousand years younger. So scholars could finally compare. They found that the ancient scroll largely agrees with the later copies, although it has many small differences in spelling and wording. For historians, that is a rare window into how ancient scribes copied, and sometimes changed, the texts they treasured.

Mystery number four: who hid them? Near the caves are the ruins of an ancient settlement. Archaeologists dug there in the years that followed. They found a long room that some called a writing room, with remains of inkwells. They found several stepped pools that many interpret as ritual baths. And they found pottery very similar to the jars in the caves. Some of the caves are so close to the settlement that you can see them from the ruins. Many scholars think a Jewish religious group lived there, collected or wrote many of the scrolls, and hid them in the caves, perhaps when Roman soldiers arrived during a revolt in the first century. Others think the scrolls came from Jerusalem, or from several different groups, and were carried into the desert to keep them safe. This is still debated, and the evidence does not settle it. Some archaeologists even suggest the settlement was a farm, a pottery workshop or a small fortress, and that its link to the scrolls is weaker than it looks. One scroll makes the mystery even stranger. It is not written on leather, but on thin sheets of copper. It is a list of hidden treasure: gold and silver buried in sixty-four places. No one has ever found that treasure, and scholars still argue about whether it was ever real.

Mystery number five: how did four of them end up for sale in a newspaper? In 1954, a small advertisement appeared in an American newspaper. It offered four Dead Sea Scrolls for sale. They were the same four scrolls the head of the monastery had bought years earlier, and had carried all the way to the United States. Through a middleman, a buyer acting for Israel quietly paid a quarter of a million dollars for them. The buyer was the son of the same professor who had bought the other three scrolls in 1947. Father and son, years apart, had brought the first seven scrolls back together. For years, only a small team of scholars was allowed to study many of the fragments, and publication moved slowly. Frustration grew. Finally, in 1991, photographs of the scrolls were made available to researchers everywhere. Today, many of the scrolls are kept in a special museum building in Jerusalem, with a white roof shaped like the lid of one of those clay jars. Even now, they are fragile. Light and changing air can damage them, so the originals are shown only for short periods, and the museum often displays careful copies instead, while the real scrolls rest in the dark again, just as they did in the caves.

So the next time you hear a stone tumble into the dark, remember the shepherd in the desert, the scribes who wrote by lamplight, and the scrolls that waited in silence for two thousand years.
